blocks.text: Equations of motion describe the motion of an object in terms of its three kinematic variables: velocity (v), position (s) and time (t). There are three ways to pair these variables, velocity-time, position-time and velocity-position, called in this order the first, second and third equations of motion. These equations can only be applied to objects moving in a straight line with constant acceleration.
Derivation of the first equation of motion

Suppose a body moves with uniform acceleration a along a straight line with an initial velocity vi, and its velocity changes from vi to a final value vf in a time interval t. The acceleration produced during this interval is a = (vf - vi)/t. Rearranging, vf - vi = at, or vf = vi + at ... (2.11). This is the first equation of motion: it relates the final velocity attained by a body to its initial velocity and the time interval t when it moves with constant acceleration a.
Derivation of the first equation by the graphical method

Let the velocity of a body at point A be vi, which changes to vf at point B in time t (Fig. 2.5). A perpendicular BD is drawn from B to the x-axis and another perpendicular BE from B to the y-axis, so that OA = vi (initial velocity) and BD = vf (final velocity). From the graph, BD = BC + CD = BC + OA (as OA = CD); therefore vf = BC + vi ... (2.12). The value of BC is found from the slope of the line AB, which equals the acceleration a: a = BC/AC, and as AC = t, a = BC/t, or BC = at ... (2.13). Combining (2.12) and (2.13), vf = at + vi, or vf = vi + at.

blocks.alt: Velocity-time graph. The straight line AB rises from A on the velocity axis (OA = vi) to B (BD = vf). Dashed lines run from E to B, from A to C (length t) and from B down through C to D on the time axis; a double arrow beside BD marks vf.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.5: Velocity-time graph (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.5).

blocks.text: Derivation of the second equation of motion

Suppose a body moving with uniform acceleration a along a straight line has initial velocity vi, which becomes vf after a time interval t, and covers a distance S in a particular direction during t. From the definition of velocity as the rate of change of displacement, velocity = displacement / time, or displacement = velocity x time. If the velocity is not constant we use the average velocity instead: displacement = average velocity x time = ((final velocity + initial velocity)/2) x time, so S = ((vi + vf)/2) t. Using the first equation, S = ((vi + vi + at)/2) t = ((2 vi + at)/2) t, so 2S = 2 vi t + a t^2, or S = vi t + (1/2) a t^2 ... (2.14). This is the second equation of motion.
Derivation of the second equation by the graphical method

On the velocity-time graph of a body with initial velocity vi that attains vf in time t while moving with constant acceleration a and covering a displacement S (Fig. 2.6), the distance travelled is S = v x t, which is the area of the figure OABD: S = (area of the rectangle OACD) + (area of the triangle ABC) = (OA x OD) + (1/2)(AC x BC). As OA = vi and OD = AC = t, S = vi x t + (1/2)(t x BC); and BC = at from the first equation, so S = vi t + (1/2)(t x at), or S = vi t + (1/2) a t^2.

blocks.alt: Velocity-time graph. The straight line AB rises from A on the velocity axis (OA = vi) to B (BD = vf). Dashed lines run from E to B, from A to C (length t) and from B down through C to D on the time axis; a double arrow beside BD marks vf.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.6: Velocity-time graph (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.6).

blocks.text: Derivation of the third equation of motion

Consider a body moving along a straight line with initial velocity vi that attains a final value vf in time t, with displacement S during this interval. Then displacement = ((initial velocity + final velocity)/2) x time, S = ((vi + vf)/2) t, or 2S = (vi + vf) t ... (2.15). From the first equation vf = vi + at, so t = (vf - vi)/a. Putting this value of t in (2.15), 2S = (vi + vf)((vf - vi)/a), or 2aS = vf^2 - vi^2. This is the third equation of motion.
Derivation of the third equation by the graphical method

In the speed-time graph (Fig. 2.7) the total distance S travelled by the body is the area OABD under the graph, a trapezium: S = (1/2)(sum of parallel sides) x height = (1/2)(OA + BD) x OD. Since OA = vi, BD = vf and OD = t, S = (1/2)(vi + vf) x t. From the first equation t = (vf - vi)/a; putting t in the equation, S = (1/2)(vi + vf)((vf - vi)/a), or 2aS = vf^2 - vi^2 ... (2.16).

blocks.alt: Velocity-time graph. The straight line AB rises from A on the velocity axis (OA = vi) to B (BD = vf). Dashed lines run from E to B, from A to C (length t) and from B down through C to D on the time axis; a double arrow beside BD marks vf.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.7: Velocity-time graph (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.7).

blocks.text: The equations of motion are useful for problems of linear motion with uniform acceleration, when an object moves along a straight line. If its direction of motion does not change, all the vector quantities can be manipulated like scalars: the initial velocity is taken as positive and a negative sign is assigned to quantities whose direction is opposite to that of the initial velocity. In the absence of air resistance, all objects in free fall at the surface of the Earth move toward the Earth with a uniform acceleration, the acceleration due to gravity, denoted by g, whose average value at the Earth's surface is taken as 9.8 m s^-2 in the downward direction. The equations for uniformly accelerated motion also apply to the free-fall motion of an object by replacing a by g.

blocks.title: Example 2.2
blocks.text: A car travelling at 10 m s^-1 accelerates uniformly at 2 m s^-2. Calculate its velocity after 5 s. Solution: vi = 10 m s^-1, a = 2 m s^-2, t = 5 s. Using the first equation, vf = vi + at = 10 m s^-1 + 2 m s^-2 x 5 s = 10 m s^-1 + 10 m s^-1 = 20 m s^-1.

blocks.title: Example 2.3
blocks.text: A car travels with initial velocity 15 m s^-1 and accelerates at 2 m s^-2 for 4 seconds. Find its displacement. Solution: vi = 15 m s^-1, a = 2 m s^-2, t = 4 s. By the second equation S = vi t + (1/2) a t^2 = (15 m s^-1 x 4 s) + (1/2)(2 m s^-2)(16 s^2) = 76 m.

blocks.title: Example 2.4
blocks.text: In a short-distance race a car starts from rest and reaches 300 km h^-1 after covering 0.45 km at constant acceleration. Find the acceleration. Solution: vi = 0; vf = 300 km h^-1 = (300 x 1000)/(60 x 60) m s^-1 = 250/3 m s^-1; S = 0.45 km = 450 m. Using the third equation vf^2 - vi^2 = 2aS: (250/3 m s^-1)^2 - 0 = 2 x a x 450 m, so a = 6944.4 m^2 s^-2 / 900 m = 7.72 m s^-2.
